open-question.question: What function-derived subject does the bootstrap commit carry, given it has no milestone id to serve as descriptor (a marker such as Workflow-bootstrap: with what descriptor), and is the commit subject-only like the other setup skills or does it carry a body naming which files were created versus preserved?

Does the git work-tree check run before or after the Python check, does a project failing both get one combined stop message or two separate stops on successive runs, and does the git check run on every invocation including a re-run on an already-bootstrapped project, as the Python check does?
open-question.alternative: Keep step 1 as it is and add the git work-tree check as a new step right after it, before state detection. Both checks run on every invocation. Each check stops on its own with its own message, so a project that fails both is stopped by the Python check first and hears about git only on the next run. It extends the existing step 1 template without changing it. Each stop keeps its single four-part message unchanged, the Python check's wording and position stay as they are, and a re-run on an already-bootstrapped project gets both checks the same way. A project missing both prerequisites needs two failed runs before it learns everything it must fix. The order puts the rarer failure (no suitable python3) ahead of the one a fresh empty directory is most likely to hit (not a git repository).

Put the git work-tree check first, ahead of the Python check, with both still running on every invocation before state detection. Each check stops on its own with its own message, so a project that fails both learns about git first and about Python on the next run. The failure most likely in a fresh directory is reported first, and it has the cheapest remedy (git init). Commit capability is also the more basic requirement, because every committing skill needs it while only the question skills need python3. Each stop still keeps its own single four-part message. Step 1 is renumbered and the Python check is no longer the opening check the skill's opening paragraph describes, so the prose and docs/skill-reference.md that present the Python check as the first thing the skill does need edits. A project failing both still needs two runs.

Run both checks on every invocation before state detection, always evaluating both, and stop once with a single message when either fails. The message covers each failing prerequisite in the four-part shape (what it looked for, what it found, the remedy) and ends with one closing line saying that a re-run completes the bootstrap. A project failing both prerequisites learns everything it must fix in one run. The order question goes away except as the order of sections in the message, which matters most for first-time users bootstrapping an empty directory. Step 1's one-check, one-message template has to be restructured into a collect-then-report step, so the Python check's stop logic and message are rewritten rather than left alone. The stop message is longer and has more branches, and how it is laid out depends on how the sibling question about git-check remedy wording settles the git message's shape.

Keep the Python check first and on every invocation. Run the git work-tree check after state detection and only on the path that will write, so a re-run on an already-bootstrapped project stops as "already initialized" without checking for git. The check is required only where it matters. A no-op re-run writes nothing and commits nothing, so it has no need for a git repository, and the scaffolding step's precondition stays next to the commit it protects. It departs from the Python check's every-invocation rule, so the two prerequisites behave differently. A re-run would no longer serve as a health check: an already-bootstrapped project that is not a git repository gets told it is initialized, and then every later committing skill fails at the commit procedure, which assumes a work tree and checks for none.

open-question.question: When the project is not a git repository, does the stop message tell the user to run git init and re-run, or does the skill offer to initialize the repository itself, and does the message follow the four-part shape of the Python stop message (what it looked for, what it found, the remedy, that a re-run completes the bootstrap)?

alternative.id: Four-part stop, user runs git init

open-question.alternative: The git check copies the step 1 Python template. It stops before any write and prints one message giving what it looked for (a git work tree at the workspace root), what it found (either the `git` executable is missing or the directory is not a work tree), the remedy that fits (install git, or run `git init` in the workspace root), and that running `/init-milestone-base-workflow` again completes the bootstrap with nothing to undo. The skill never runs `git init` itself. It matches the goal's wording "stopping before it writes anything when the project is not a git repository" and reuses a stop shape the skill already has, so the two prerequisite checks read the same. It also never prompts, so it behaves the same in a headless chain. Choosing where the repository lives stays with the user, which matters when the workspace root might be the wrong directory for it. The most common case, a fresh project with no repository yet, always costs a stop, a manual `git init`, and a second run. If the "Work-tree check strictness" question settles on stricter pass rules, the "what it found" part needs more cases, such as being inside a larger repository but not at its top level.

When no work tree is found, the skill asks the user whether to run `git init` in the workspace root. If the user agrees, it initializes the repository and continues the bootstrap in the same run. If the user declines, or no one can answer, it falls back to a four-part stop message like the Python one. Interactive users get through the common fresh-project case in one run without leaving the skill, and nothing is created without explicit consent. It adds a consent prompt that no other prerequisite check has, and that prompt cannot be answered in a headless chain. It also stretches the goal's "stopping before it writes anything": with consent, the skill creates a `.git` directory, which is outside the paths it owns. The skill would also have to handle a brand-new repository with no commits and no configured identity before its first commit could succeed.

The skill stops before any write with a single short line, for example "not a git repository — run git init and re-run /init-milestone-base-workflow". It does not follow the four-part shape and does not tell a missing `git` executable apart from a directory that is not a repository. It is the smallest runtime change. It also fits the terse console-reporting style the other committing skills use. The skill's two prerequisite checks would report failures in different shapes. When git itself is not installed, the one-line remedy is wrong, and nothing in the message says so. The user loses the found-versus-expected detail that the Python check deliberately gives.

open-question.question: When CLAUDE.md or milestones/README.md already carries uncommitted changes before the bootstrap runs (for example a CLAUDE.md just written by /init and never committed), does the bootstrap's path-scoped commit sweep those unrelated hunks into its own commit, stop before writing, or proceed and note it?

Does the bootstrap's step 6 report become the one fixed identifier-free status line the other committing skills print, with a distinct line for the already-initialized no-op path, and does the suggestion to run /init and /define-milestone-goal next survive as an advisory or get cut along with the created-versus-preserved itemization?

Beyond the three places the goal names, are the CLAUDE.md pipeline listing that tags the skill non-committing, design claim 12's "two exceptions" sentence, and the README's "one runtime prerequisite" sentence with its two host copies under scripts/hosts also updated to record git as a second prerequisite and the bootstrap as committing?
open-question.alternative: Update every place that states the bootstrap's non-committing exemption or calls Python the single runtime prerequisite. That covers the three sites the goal names and the four the question lists: the CLAUDE.md pipeline tag "non-committing" on line 51, design claim 12's "two exceptions" sentence (which drops to the one failed-run exception), README.md line 54, and its copies in scripts/hosts/claude/README.md and scripts/hosts/antigravity/README.md. It also covers the "the workflow's one runtime prerequisite" wording in docs/workflow.md line 11 and docs/skill-reference.md line 7. The host READMEs are then rebuilt into hosts/ so the drift gate still passes. No document is left contradicting the new behaviour. Design claim 12 would otherwise go on saying the bootstrap "does not commit and leaves its changes staged", and README.md would keep calling Python the only prerequisite while the bootstrap refuses to run outside a git work tree. The sites are chosen by a rule that a grep can check, not by a hand-kept list, so none is missed. That fits the milestone's aim of retiring the exemption everywhere. It touches the most files, including the user-facing README and its two host templates, so the milestone's diff and review surface grow beyond what the goal wrote. The "one runtime prerequisite" sentence has to be reworded into a two-prerequisite form in four or five places, and those rewordings must stay consistent. How the git requirement is phrased there also depends on how strict the work-tree check turns out to be (for example, whether a subdirectory of a larger repository passes).

Beyond the three sites the goal names, fix only the statements that the bootstrap does not commit: the CLAUDE.md pipeline tag and design claim 12's "two exceptions" sentence. The README's "one runtime prerequisite" sentence and its host copies stay as they are. The git check is treated as a guard against running outside a repository, not as a declared runtime prerequisite. It removes every statement that the change makes false, since both the pipeline tag and claim 12 say outright that the bootstrap does not commit. The user-facing README and the two scripts/hosts templates, which feed the published distribution repos, are left alone. The change stays close to the goal's wording. The docs end up disagreeing on what Cairn needs: the README, docs/workflow.md line 11 and docs/skill-reference.md line 7 still say Python is the one prerequisite, while the bootstrap stops with a remedy when git is missing. A user who reads the README's prerequisite section first will not learn about the git requirement until the bootstrap refuses to run. Calling git a "guard" rather than a prerequisite is a line the skill's own stop message may blur.

Update only the three places the goal names: the CLAUDE.md invariant, the exemption paragraph in docs/workflow.md, and the skill reference. The CLAUDE.md pipeline tag, design claim 12 and the README prerequisite sentences are left for a follow-up, or for a later review pass to raise. It keeps to exactly the scope the goal wrote, so the milestone's docs work is small and predictable and nothing outside the stated boundary changes. Stale, now-false statements go out with the release. CLAUDE.md would contradict itself: line 51 would still tag the skill "non-committing" under a corrected invariant on line 95. Design claim 12 would still promise an exemption that no longer exists, and the README would stay silent on the new git requirement. That defeats the goal's aim of recording that every file-changing skill commits, and it leaves a known inconsistency for someone to find later.

open-question.question: Should docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md gain a chain that starts from an empty repository with the bootstrap line, now that the bootstrap commits and a headless chain can include it without leaving files behind, or do the chains keep assuming an already-bootstrapped repository?
open-question.alternative: Add a new section to docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md, placed before "Starting a milestone", that runs from a fresh git repository through the bootstrap line and `define-milestone-goal "<goal>"`, and hands off to the existing "Starting a milestone" chain. The prose would name `git init` and `/init` as preconditions instead of putting them in the fenced block. It covers the whole headless lifecycle, from an empty repository to a finished milestone, and it shows the milestone's point: with the exemption gone, every documented chain leaves a clean tree. That makes design claim 12's clean-tree promise visible in the one page about unattended runs. It adds a new placeholder, `<goal>`, to a page whose legend defines only `<milestone_id>` and `<project-root>`, so the notation section grows too. The steps that come before the bootstrap (git init, and /init writing CLAUDE.md) cannot be `/cairn:<skill>` lines under the page's "every line is a complete invocation" rule. And if /init leaves an uncommitted CLAUDE.md, the chain's clean-tree claim holds only if the pre-existing dirty-paths question is settled so the bootstrap handles that file safely.

Add a short section, "Bootstrapping a project", whose fenced block holds just the one `claude -p "/cairn:init-milestone-base-workflow"` line, like the one-line "Finishing a milestone" section. Its sentences say to run it once in a git repository after /init, and that it leaves its scaffold committed. It documents the only skill a headless run could call that no chain covers, without adding a placeholder or breaking the page's line rule. It follows a pattern the page already uses (a one-line section), so the added text stays small and cannot go stale on define-milestone-goal's argument. It is not really a chain, so the page still gives no end-to-end path from an empty repository. A reader who wants to go on to a first milestone has to write the define-milestone-goal step themselves. Documenting a run that happens once per project arguably gains little over the README's existing setup instructions.

Put the bootstrap line at the top of the existing "Starting a milestone" chain. The skill is idempotent and stops without changes on an already-bootstrapped project, so the same chain would work on the first milestone and on every later one. No new section. One chain then works whether or not the repository has been bootstrapped, and the run cannot fail later because the scaffold is missing. It does not help an empty repository by itself: the chain's goto-next-milestone line still needs a milestone already defined, and that has to come after the bootstrap. So the chain's own precondition ("a milestone is defined and the pointer reads none") contradicts the bootstrap line in front of it. It also adds a headless model run, with its prerequisite checks, to every milestone start just to reach a no-op on every run after the first. Whether that no-op run prints a distinct line depends on how the reporting-shape question is settled.

Leave docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md without a bootstrap chain: every chain keeps assuming a bootstrapped repository, and at most one sentence in the page's opening paragraph notes that the bootstrap runs once beforehand. The milestone's scope stays at the three places the goal names. It avoids documenting a step that happens once and is usually interactive (it usually follows /init and a conversational discuss-milestone-goal) on a page meant for repeatable unattended runs. It also leaves nothing on the page that depends on how the sibling questions about subject, reporting, and dirty paths are settled. It passes up the change the goal is about: once the bootstrap commits, it is safe in a headless chain, and the page would still not say so. A reader could reasonably assume from the old exemption that the bootstrap has to stay manual. The page's claim that "every skill commits what it changes" also stays untested for the one skill that only now meets it.

open-question.question: Does the git prerequisite pass whenever the workspace root is inside any git work tree (for example a subdirectory of a larger repository), or only when the workspace root is itself the repository's top level, and does a freshly initialized repository with no commits yet pass?
